title: Sense-amp latch-time telemetry skips refresh for healthy rows
idea: Po: every read is a medical exam. A tiny time-to-digital converter on the local sense amps measures how fast each activated row resolves (faster = more charge left); rows with ample margin set a skip counter so their next one or two scheduled refreshes are dropped, and VRT cells are caught in the act.
why: Fact 3: measured rather than worst-case retention lets 70-90% of refreshes be skipped under real workloads, returning bandwidth and idle power.

title: Gear-shift bitline restore through stepped reservoir rails
idea: Random stimulus 'bicycle gears': climb the hill in small steps instead of one strain. During refresh the sense amp swings bitlines to VARY in four steps via switched on-die reservoir capacitors (0.25/0.5/0.75 VARY) that are recharged by the previous row's discharge, instead of one hard swing from the rail; refresh has timing slack, so the slower adiabatic swing costs no bandwidth.
why: Stepwise charging dissipates ~CV^2/N rather than CV^2/2, so refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, fact 3) falls ~50-70% without touching the cell.

title: Insect-drone hyperdimensional memory in rarely refreshed banks
idea: Tiny drones use hyperdimensional computing, where items are 10,000-bit random vectors that stay recognizable with 10-30% bit flips. Hold the associative item and class hypervectors in banks refreshed only when raw BER reaches ~1%, re-bundling vectors from recent samples now and then.
why: Fact 3: for HDC workloads refresh energy and ECC almost vanish and 1% cell BER costs no accuracy, so cheaper, leakier cells can be used.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO buried wordline trades swing for higher Vt
idea: Insert a ~3 nm ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 layer into the buried-wordline gate stack, capacitance-matched to the channel. The internal gate voltage is then amplified (body factor m<1), and swing drops to ~40-45 mV/dec in the operating window. Spend that gain on a higher Vt at the same Ion, not on lower voltage.
why: Over a 0.9 V gate window, going from 65 to 45 mV/dec cuts Ioff by about 10^(0.9/0.045 - 0.9/0.065), roughly 1e6, at equal Ion. Even a tenth of that removes the subthreshold part of the 13 fA tail (fact 3).

title: Negative-capacitance gate stack enabling 1.5 V wordline access transistor
idea: Po: the gate amplifies its own voltage. Insert a thin doped-HfO2 negative-capacitance layer in series with the access gate dielectric so subthreshold swing drops below 60 mV/dec in the operating window, letting the wordline swing about -0.3 to 1.5 V instead of -0.5 to 3 V at the same on/off ratio.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor and fact 3: halving wordline swing cuts wordline CV^2 ~4x, shrinks the pumps (fact 7) and adds ~10x off-current margin.

title: Asymmetric air-gap underlap kills GIDL at the storage junction
idea: IFR: no field exists where the leak is born. Form an air-gap spacer and gate underlap only on the storage-node side of the access transistor (angled deposition and etch), removing the gate-to-storage-junction overlap field that drives GIDL while the bitline side keeps overlap for drive current.
why: Fact 3: GIDL dominates the tail under negative wordline bias; removing the overlap field could cut tail leakage ~10x and allow 256 ms+ refresh.

title: Deciduous shedding: let clean backed pages decay unrefreshed
idea: Trees drop leaves in winter rather than pay to maintain them; the OS marks rows holding clean page-cache or model-weight copies that also live on SSD with a per-row 'deciduous' bit, refresh is disabled on them during idle, and a canary/ECC check on first access triggers refetch from storage if they have decayed.
why: In servers 30-50% of DRAM is clean cache; dropping its refresh cuts idle refresh energy roughly proportionally and frees refresh bandwidth.

title: Railway wheel re-profiling: per-cell charge injection retunes leaky transistors
idea: Adapted from underfloor wheel lathes that re-profile train wheels without removing them: for each cell flagged as leaky, a high-field write sequence injects charge into that access transistor's drain-side spacer, relieving its gate-edge field or raising its local threshold until leakage meets spec; it can be repeated in the field.
why: Repairs individual tail cells (fact 3) without spare rows or global bias changes, so the tail is trimmed as it appears and the whole array refreshes at the strong-cell rate.

title: Four-pocket mirror-bit storage on both faces of channel sheets
idea: IFR: one gate crossing holds four bits. Each wordline crossing of a thin vertical oxide-semiconductor sheet stores charge in four spatially separate nitride-nanodot pockets (source-side and drain-side on front and back faces, with independent front and back gates), read by swapping source/drain direction as in mirror-bit NROM.
why: Constraint: 4 bits per crossing x 8 cheap tiers is ~20x bits per footprint versus 6F^2, leaving margin for ≥10x per dollar after process overhead.

title: Eliminate per-cell access transistors: CCD recirculating memory from university nanofab
idea: Build a three-phase surface-channel CCD (two poly levels, 2 um contact lithography, standard university processing) in which data circulate as charge packets past a regenerating sense stage each lap; no cell has its own access transistor or junction leak path, and each lap is the refresh. Target streaming weight memory where access is sequential anyway.
why: Removes the per-bit access device and most periphery; dark-current-limited retention plus regeneration each lap; EUV-free and demonstrable in a university fab within months.

title: Majority-value bitline parking during long idle
idea: Time shift from ns-scale active behaviour to seconds-long standby: when a subarray idles >1 ms, a per-subarray ones-counter (updated on writes) decides whether most cells hold '1' or '0' and bitlines are parked at VARY or ground instead of VARY/2, so the majority of cells see ~0 V drain-source and stop subthreshold leaking; minority cells get a shorter refresh bin.
why: Idle refresh energy (fact 3, 16-33% of idle power): data skew (zeros dominate sparse ML tensors) lets 70-90% of cells stop channel leakage, extending effective standby retention ~2-3x.

title: Image-sensor pinned-photodiode storage node with a transfer gate
idea: Adapted from the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: store the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, isolated from every Si/SiO2 interface, and move it to a floating diffusion through a transfer gate. A source follower reads it like a 4T pixel, so ~1-3k electrons suffice instead of ~30k.
why: Pinned photodiodes reach dark currents of a few electrons per second (~aA) at room temperature, ~10^4x below the 13 fA tail (fact 3); retention of seconds nearly removes refresh and the need for a 60-75:1 capacitor (fact 1), at 3-4 transistors per cell.

title: Image-sensor pinned photodiode recast as buried, interface-free DRAM storage well
idea: Borrow the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: store the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well under a p+ pinning layer, read out through a transfer gate onto a floating diffusion exactly like a 4T pixel. The stored charge never touches a Si/SiO2 interface, so interface-trap SRH generation (the source of most of the <=13 fA tail) is shut off; a deep-trench vertical pinned well, as in stacked global-shutter pixels, supplies ~8-15k electrons.
why: Fact 3: CIS dark current is ~1-10 e-/s per pixel versus ~8x10^4 e-/s for a 13 fA DRAM tail cell; even a 100x leakage cut stretches refresh from 64 ms to seconds, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss 10-100x.

title: Pinned storage well: the image-sensor trick buries the bit
idea: Inverts 'the bit must sit on a metal-contacted capacitor': store electrons in a buried n-well under a p+ surface pinning layer (the pinned-photodiode structure from CMOS image sensors, built as a deep vertical well), moved in and out by a transfer gate to a floating-diffusion sense node; the pinning layer keeps interface traps filled with holes so they cannot generate leakage.
why: Pinned wells show orders of magnitude lower dark current than surface or junction nodes, so retention moves from 64 ms toward minutes (fact 3) with no capacitor tower (fact 1); trade-off is a small well and charge-transfer read.

title: Thin p-well with deep minority-carrier sink beneath the array
idea: Above ~70 C, diffusion current from carriers generated in the neutral p-well (Ea ~ Eg ~1.1 eV) overtakes depletion generation, and any electron generated within a diffusion length can wander into a storage node. Thin the array p-well to ~0.3 um and place a strongly biased buried n+ collector plane just below. Thermally generated electrons are swept away vertically before they reach storage nodes, the image-sensor vertical-overflow-drain trick.
why: The generation volume feeding storage nodes shrinks ~10-30x. This matters most in hot HBM stacks at 85-95 C, where refresh doubles. Expect a 2-5x retention gain at high temperature (facts 3, 6).

title: One shallow p+ pinning implant mask ends storage-node surface leakage
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x standard SA x in-array x Si x exactly one added implant mask. Borrowing the image-sensor pinned photodiode, a shallow p+ layer over the exposed storage-node diffusion pins the Si/SiO2 interface in hole accumulation so its interface states stop generating current.
why: Pinning cut CIS dark current ~100x; surface generation is a major tail source, so expect 3-10x lower tail leakage and proportional refresh savings (fact 3) for one mask.

title: Watchmaker's escapement: tunnel-diode Goto pair keeps cells latched
idea: An escapement gives a pendulum a tiny kick each swing so it never stops. Stack two nanoscale Esaki tunnel diodes (a Goto pair) on each storage node between plate rails; their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages sustained by pA valley current, so charge is continuously restored with no refresh at near-1T cell area.
why: Eliminates refresh (fact 3) at perhaps 1.3-1.5x cell area versus ~20x for 6T SRAM; standby stays ~pA per cell if the diode peak-to-valley ratio is high.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode pair self-restores each bit without refresh
idea: Effect: interband tunneling negative differential resistance. Two nanoscale p++/n++ Ge (or SiGe) Esaki diodes stacked in series on the storage node form a Goto pair; a pA standby current biases them so the node has two stable voltages that actively restore against leakage, giving a refresh-free 1T2D cell barely larger than 1T1C.
why: Refresh eliminated (fact 3) at near-DRAM density; trade-off is pA/cell standby current, which must beat 46 fJ/bit refresh.

title: Zero refresh energy from the supply: Esaki tunnel-diode latch storage node
idea: Limit: holding data may cost no refresh cycles at all. Hang a pair of series Esaki tunnel diodes from each storage node to a standby rail. Their negative-differential-resistance load line gives two stable node voltages. Picoamp tunnel current continuously compensates leakage, so the cell latches like static memory in a DRAM footprint.
why: Fact 3: turns ~46 fJ/bit of refresh energy into a static picoamp hold current and frees the 10-20% of bandwidth refresh consumes. Risks: diode peak-to-valley ratio at nm scale and standby current density.

title: Supermarket expiry dating places perishable data in unrefreshed banks
idea: OS/runtime allocators tag buffers with a use-by time, as a supermarket dates perishables. Activations, KV-cache pages, packet buffers and staging tensors go to banks with refresh permanently disabled whose certified retention (e.g., 250 ms at 85 C) exceeds the tag. Expired data is recomputed or re-fetched.
why: Zero refresh power for the perishable share of capacity, often a large fraction of AI accelerator memory. It recovers the 10-20% refresh bandwidth there.

title: Magnify the value of persistence: kill AI checkpoint memory overhead
idea: Sell non-volatile DRAM-class modules to AI training clusters as checkpoint-free memory: training state persists through power events in place, eliminating host-DRAM staging buffers and periodic checkpoint copies.
why: Recovers ~10-20% of cluster memory capacity and step time; creates a premium launch market that funds NV-DRAM lines.

title: Pipeline cathodic protection: guard junctions intercept stray carriers
idea: Adapted from cathodic protection, where a sacrificial anode takes corrosion current instead of the pipe: run a shallow, reverse-biased n+ guard stripe between storage-node rows, tied to a collector rail, so minority electrons generated in the bulk or injected by hammered neighbor rows are collected before reaching a storage node.
why: Part of the leakage tail and much row-hammer charge loss is carrier diffusion through the substrate; a collector that grabs it could cut bulk-generated leakage several-fold (fact 3) and raise row-hammer thresholds (fact 9).

title: Refresh-off banks for tensors that die before they decay
idea: First principle: if data lives for less than the guaranteed retention (64 ms, with a median of seconds), refreshing it is pure waste. Patch an open accelerator runtime and an FPGA HBM/DDR5 controller so activations, in-flight gradients and per-step scratch go to banks that get no per-bank REF commands. A hardware 32 ms age watchdog turns refresh back on if any page outlives its lease. About $600k and 18 months of engineering.
why: AI working sets are dominated by short-lived tensors. Suppressing refresh on half the banks returns ~5-10% bandwidth and half the refresh energy at 32-64 Gb densities (fact 3), with zero fab changes.

title: HBM stack thermal gradient: long-lived data sinks to cooler dies
idea: Scale shift to the stack: HBM layers run at different temperatures (top dies 5-15 C hotter), so the controller sets a per-die refresh interval from on-die sensors and migrates long-lived, rarely accessed pages to the coolest layers while frequently touched (naturally refreshed) data lives in the hottest ones.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): retention halves per ~10 C, so per-die binning and placement cut refresh ~30-50% in unmodified Si/Cu HBM.

title: Decay-tolerant page cache re-faults from flash instead of refreshing
idea: Clean pages (file cache, model weights loaded from NVMe, read-only container layers) have an authoritative copy on storage, so they need probable, not guaranteed, retention. Keep them in banks at 8x relaxed refresh with a per-line CRC. On a mismatch the kernel drops the page and re-faults it from storage. A kernel patch plus controller CRC fits easily within $1M and 18 months.
why: Clean pages often fill 30-60% of server DRAM; cutting their refresh 8x removes a large share of refresh energy (fact 3) at no capacity cost.

title: Z80 R-register reborn: inference weight sweeps certified as refresh
idea: Revive the Zilog Z80's trick of refreshing DRAM during opcode fetch: the memory controller tracks which rows were read within the retention window and suppresses explicit refresh for them. LLM inference streams every weight row once per token (~20-50 ms), so the scheduler orders weight reads to touch every row within tREFW and weight regions in HBM become self-refreshing.
why: Removes most explicit refresh for weight-resident HBM (facts 3, 5); weights often fill 50-80% of capacity, so refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax fall roughly in proportion.

title: Airlock two-gate pillar using stack-effect isolation
idea: Random stimulus 'airlock': two doors that are never open together. Split the vertical access pillar's gate into two independently driven segments (upper/lower wordlines, no added footprint); in retention both are off and the floating mid-channel node self-biases, giving the storage-side segment negative Vgs and near-zero Vds (the stack effect), while both open together within ~1 ns for access.
why: Stack effect cuts subthreshold leakage ~10-30x and suppresses DIBL on the storage side, pulling the <=13 fA tail toward ~1 fA so the refresh interval rises 8x+ (fact 3) at zero footprint cost in a vertical-channel cell.

title: Water-utility pressure management: store a lower '1' level during standby
idea: Water utilities cut leaks by lowering night pressure because crack flow rises faster than linearly with pressure. On self-refresh entry, rewrite rows with a '1' of ~0.75 VARY instead of full VARY; GIDL and trap-assisted junction leakage fall super-linearly with storage-node voltage, so tail cells lose charge more slowly than the signal shrinks, and full levels are restored on exit.
why: Net retention gain of ~1.5-3x for GIDL-dominated tail cells plus lower CV^2 per standby refresh (facts 3, 10).

title: Eliminate the leakage tail: per-cell Vt trim via charge-trap back gate
idea: Give each access transistor a thin back gate with a nitride charge-trap layer; at final test the tester finds the leakiest 0.1-1% of cells and Fowler-Nordheim-programs electrons into their back-gate trap, raising Vt 200-300 mV permanently. The tail cells that set the refresh rate are trimmed to the median.
why: Refresh interval is set by the worst ~1e-6 of cells; collapsing the tail by 1-2 decades lets tREFW stretch 4-16x, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss proportionally (fact 3).

title: Factory-injected nitride charge trims Vt of only the leakiest cells
idea: Time shift from ns operation to decade-long stored charge: the access transistor's spacer liner includes a SiN trap layer, and at wafer test cells found in the leakage tail receive a one-time high-field injection via their wordline/bitline that permanently stores electrons, raising their Vt ~150-250 mV for the product's 10-year life.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): flattening the worst ~0.1% of cells lets the refresh interval rise 4-8x using only Si and N; risk is trapped-charge loss at 85 C over 10 years.

title: IBM's cryogenic dream made cheap with LNG terminal cold
idea: IBM's cryogenic Josephson computer died on refrigeration cost. At 77 K, DRAM access-transistor leakage drops by ~1e5-1e6 and refresh effectively vanishes. Site memory-heavy racks at LNG regasification terminals, which normally dump ~0.8 MJ of cold per kg into seawater, and use a nitrogen loop to hold DRAM pools at 77-100 K.
why: Eliminates refresh power and the refresh bandwidth tax, and lets access transistors use a lower Vt for speed. Cooling comes from waste cold, and leakier dies scrapped today become usable supply.

title: Smart-dust Esaki-diode latch that makes the DRAM cell static
idea: Smart dust has no energy budget for refresh. Hang two series tunnel (Esaki) diodes between the rails at the storage node; their negative-differential-resistance curve gives two stable points near 0 and VDD, so pA-level diode currents hold the node instead of letting it decay, while reads and writes still use the normal access transistor.
why: Fact 3: refresh disappears (the cell becomes static like tunnel-diode SRAM) at a fraction of SRAM area; risk is building matched nanoscale tunnel diodes inside a 6F^2 footprint and their standby current.

title: Nickel-seeded lateral crystallization makes single-grain transistors in every 3D tier
idea: Ni: in a stacked 3D DRAM, deposit amorphous Si for each tier and open one DUV-defined Ni seed window per row; a 500-550 C anneal sweeps a NiSi2 front laterally (metal-induced lateral crystallization), leaving long single-grain needles where lateral access transistors are placed, followed by Ni gettering.
why: Attacks the lateral-transistor blocker of 3D DRAM (fact 2) with near-single-crystal leakage at low thermal budget, without epitaxial superlattices or EUV; residual Ni is the leakage risk.

title: Inside-out cell: access transistor grown inside the capacitor's hollow core
idea: Rearrange inside and outside: form the cylindrical storage capacitor first as an open shell, then grow a vertical gate-all-around channel up its hollow core so the capacitor's inner electrode is the transistor's drain, with no landing pad or buried contact between them. The wordline wraps the channel inside the cylinder.
why: Removes the storage contact/landing pad, a dominant leakage and resistance site (facts 3, 7), and folds transistor into capacitor footprint (~4F2), improving both retention tail and area.

title: Buried minority-carrier collector layer sweeps substrate electrons
idea: Worse at 125 C: let thermally generated electrons in the hot substrate diffuse up into storage nodes. Flip: implant a biased buried n+ collector plane a few microns below the array that sweeps diffusion current away before it reaches the storage junctions.
why: Removes the diffusion component of hot leakage (fact 3), which dominates above ~100 C; ~3-5x retention at 125 C.

title: ZettaCore molecules as built-in tunnel barrier and capacitor
idea: ZettaCore's porphyrin charge-storage molecules died on electrolyte integration and temperature limits. Covalently anchor ferrocene or porphyrin redox molecules to a TiN nanopillar through a rigid alkyl tether of chosen length, inside a solid polymer electrolyte. The tether's tunneling distance sets the self-discharge time, each CH2 unit multiplying it ~3x, so the molecular layer is both a multi-electron capacitor and its own leak-limiting access barrier.
why: Redox monolayers hold ~1e14 e/cm2, beating the MIM capacitor charge wall, and retention can be tuned from seconds to minutes by tether length. Speculative mainly because of write speed.

title: Coin-cell nanobattery bit holds voltage as state of charge
idea: Shrink coin-cell battery manufacturing to a solid-state Li-free nanobattery per cell (e.g., proton or Ag+ intercalation electrodes). The bit is its open-circuit voltage, read non-destructively through a gain transistor and written by a short current pulse.
why: Zero refresh: a battery holds its voltage for years by electrochemistry, not by isolating charge. Speed and endurance are the speculative risks.

title: Grow on reusable single-crystal wafers, laser-lift-off the memory film
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: grow single-crystal wide-gap channel layers (GaN, AlGaN or Ga2O3) on sapphire or bulk-oxide growth wafers, bond them to cheap glass panels, and laser-lift-off the film as in micro-LED and flexible-OLED production; the expensive growth wafer is repolished and reused 20-50 times.
why: Delivers single-crystal, low-leakage access channels (Fact 3) at glass-panel cost; cuts substrate cost and scarce-crystal demand per bit by >10x.

title: Laminated-glass hBN floating-graphene bit with sub-ns super-injection
idea: Like safety glass laminated around a PVB interlayer, stack a graphene charge layer between hBN tunnel barriers over a 2D MoS2 channel. Writes use the 2D-enhanced hot-carrier super-injection that reaches sub-ns programming, so the cell is read like a gain cell.
why: Zero refresh: charge behind 6 eV hBN stays for years. The open question is DRAM-class endurance, so the risk is honestly high.

title: Surface-acoustic-wave wordline gates 2D channels on piezoelectric substrate
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: on lithium niobate or AlScN-on-sapphire, a GHz surface acoustic wave launched along a row carries a piezoelectric potential that momentarily opens MoS2 access channels as it passes, so the 'wordline' is a travelling wave, not a charged metal line. Between waves the channels sit deeply off with no static gate bias; row latency is transit time (~30 ns per 100 um).
why: Eliminates wordline CV2 and negative-bias pumps (Facts 7, 10) and row-hammer coupling (Fact 9) while keeping off-state leakage minimal (Fact 3); coupling strength is speculative.

title: Retention-DLTS fingerprints the defect species behind the leakage tail
idea: Treat a commodity DRAM as a billion-pixel deep-level transient spectrometer. Measure each weak cell's retention time against temperature (the Arrhenius slope gives trap energy) and against wordline/plate bias (the field-enhancement factor separates Poole-Frenkel, phonon-assisted tunneling and GIDL). Cluster the signatures across vendors and lots to name the dominant defect species (Fe-B, vacancy-oxygen, interface Pb centers).
why: Knowing which defect sets the 13 fA tail tells fabs which fix (gettering, passivation or field relief) buys the most refresh relief. A two-person lab with FPGA testers and thermal chambers can do it for <$500k in 18 months (fact 3).

title: TOPCon passivating contact replaces the implanted storage-node junction
idea: Solar TOPCon contacts reach saturation currents of ~5 fA/cm^2 by placing a 1.5 nm tunnel oxide between crystalline silicon and heavily doped poly-Si, so the defective metallurgical junction sits outside the crystal. Form the storage-node contact as a tunnel-oxide/n+ poly stack on an undoped channel tip: by reciprocity, a contact with near-zero recombination J0 also has near-zero generation (leakage) current.
why: Junction generation is a core part of the <=13 fA tail (fact 3); a contact that gave solar cells 10-100x lower J0 could cut junction leakage ~10x and extend refresh 4-10x.

title: Vacuum-flask isolation: hydrogen-anneal voids float storage junctions above nothing
idea: A thermos keeps heat in by surrounding it with nothing. Etch a dense array of tiny holes with Cl2/HBr plasma beneath each storage-node region and anneal in H2 at ~1100 C so silicon surface migration seals them into a continuous buried void ('empty space in silicon'); the storage junction sits on vacuum, with no HF release etch or fluorinated gas.
why: Eliminates most of the junction's bottom-area depletion volume and its generation leakage toward the substrate (fact 3): ~2-5x lower junction leakage.

title: Ultra-thin fully depleted body shrinks thermal generation volume
idea: Worse at 125 C: give the access device a large depleted silicon volume that generates carriers at mid-gap traps. Flip: thin the vertical channel to a 4-5 nm shell on an oxide core so the generating volume is ~50x smaller and quantum confinement widens the effective gap.
why: Generation leakage, the dominant term hot (fact 3), down ~20-50x at 125 C.

title: Magnetostrictive NEMS relay access with vacuum-gap off state
idea: Effect: magnetostriction. A Galfenol (FeGa) nanobeam above each storage contact elongates in the field of a current-carrying wordline and touches a Ru contact pad; with no current a ~5 nm sealed vacuum gap separates node and bitline, giving zero channel leakage; GHz mechanical resonance at 10 nm scale keeps actuation in ns.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ideal mechanical off state leaves only capacitor-dielectric leakage, retention minutes to hours; actuation is by current, avoiding the 3 V gate swing (fact 10). Risk: contact wear at 1e15 cycles.

title: Self-clearing film-capacitor electrode isolates leaky capacitor defects automatically
idea: Metallized-film power capacitors survive dielectric flaws because a local breakdown vaporizes the ultrathin electrode around the flaw, isolating it. Make the DRAM top plate locally ultrathin (2-3 nm TiN or Ru) over the high-k so a forming pulse at test burns open a nanometric hole around any leakage hot spot, removing that path while losing <1% of the cell's capacitor area.
why: Dielectric leakage defects set part of the retention tail and block thinner/higher-k films (facts 1, 3); self-clearing converts defect-tail cells into normal ones and lets the film be thinned for more fF.

title: 2050 quantum engineer: superconducting loops with nanowire-cryotron access
idea: A 2050 quantum-computing engineer already has 4 K space to spare. Each bit is a persistent current in a NbN loop, selected by a nanowire cryotron (nTron) that a small gate current drives normal; loops hold current indefinitely, so there is no leakage or refresh, and switching costs attojoules.
why: Device-level access energy drops 100-1000x and refresh is zero; fits as working memory next to cryogenic processors where cooling already exists.

title: Eliminate electronic charge storage: solid-electrolyte proton-intercalation bit
idea: Store the bit as protons intercalated into a 5 nm WO3 channel, written through a thin inorganic proton conductor (e.g., hydrogenated HfO2) with ~10 ns pulses; at zero bias the ions are immobile, so nothing leaks, and reads measure channel conductance non-destructively. Electrons are not the stored quantity, so they cannot leak away.
why: Eliminates refresh and destructive read (facts 3, 8); open risks are ionic-cycling endurance and speed versus DRAM's unlimited-endurance target.

title: Van der Waals semi-floating-gate cell with hBN tunnel window
idea: Po: the storage node is a sheet of graphite. Stack MoS2 channel / hBN / multilayer graphene floating gate, where the floating gate also touches the drain through a thin WSe2 p-n junction window: writes inject charge through the junction in ~ns at 1-2 V, hBN holds it for seconds, and read senses the channel nondestructively.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 8: no capacitor, nondestructive read and retention far beyond 64 ms; risk is wafer-scale 2D stacking.

title: Retention-first respin of a legacy DRAM node
idea: Reverse the optimization target on a fully depreciated 2x/3x nm DRAM line: give up ~30% density and spend the area on a longer recessed channel, thicker gate oxide at the storage-node overlap and a fatter capacitor, so the leakage tail drops ~10x and Cs rises ~1.5x. The part ships with ~1 s refresh as a low-idle-power LPDDR or CXL capacity tier.
why: Self-refresh power (fact 3) falls ~15x, and a paid-off line (depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) keeps cost per bit competitive despite lower density.

title: Oxide retention gate in series with a fast silicon access transistor
idea: Put an oxide-semiconductor transistor in series with each Si access device, driven by a per-bank retention line. That line stays on while the bank is active, so it adds no switching delay, and turns off when the bank idles; the Si device does all the fast switching.
why: Keeps DDR timing in active mode while idle banks reach oxide-level leakage (~1e-19 A). Self-refresh in idle (16-33% of idle power) disappears.

title: Power-switch fabs make memory switches: SiC-access DRAM tier
idea: Reverse the role of a power transistor: run underused 150/200 mm 4H-SiC MOSFET lines (idle after the EV slowdown) at their finest ~0.35-0.5 um rules to make 1T1C cells with SiC access transistors and trench capacitors. SiC's 3.3 eV gap gives intrinsic carrier density ~1e-9 cm-3, so off-current is low enough that retention reaches minutes to hours, as 1990s SiC DRAM demonstrations showed.
why: Uses existing SiC fabs (several in the U.S.) with no EUV to make a near refresh-free DRAM-class tier (fact 3); density is ~100x below leading DRAM, so it serves idle-dominated capacity, not bulk.

title: Magnify the gate count: two series wordlines per vertical pillar
idea: Stack two independently driven gate-all-around segments along each vertical access pillar; both turn on for access, but in standby the intermediate node self-biases to give the upper device negative Vgs (stack effect), dropping subthreshold leakage 10-30x.
why: Leakage tail down 10-30x at 4F^2 using only extra height; refresh interval ~8x.

title: Optane's selector drift turned into DRAM retention
idea: In 3D XPoint, the ovonic threshold switch's threshold voltage drifted upward with log-time after each firing, which eroded read margins. Use two back-to-back OTS films as the access device of a crosspoint 1S1C capacitor cell. After each access the threshold drifts up, so the selector's off-state leakage falls as the stored bit ages. Each access or refresh re-fires the selector, which resets its state.
why: Transistor-free, stackable 4F2 crosspoint DRAM (attacks the 3D DRAM blocker and litho cost). Because drift makes leakage fall over time instead of sitting at a fixed tail, refresh is claimed to be ~10x longer than in half-select-limited crosspoint designs.

title: Pyrolytic self-cleaning oven: wordline heaters anneal VRT traps in the field
idea: Self-cleaning ovens periodically run very hot to burn off residue. In a maintenance window, migrate a bank's data, then drive current through its buried metal wordlines as resistive heaters to hold the array near 250 C for seconds, re-annealing VRT and hydrogen-related traps (as shown for NAND self-healing) before the data returns; no chemistry at all.
why: Resets the aging-driven retention tail (fact 3) so the end-of-life refresh guardband (~2x) can be dropped and VRT outliers are erased rather than mapped out.

title: Weak rows get the hottest-written data
idea: Reverse page placement: the OS uses a per-row retention map to put frequently rewritten pages (stacks, network buffers, KV-cache heads) onto the weakest rows, since every write restores them, and cold read-mostly pages onto the strongest rows. The refresh interval then follows the strong rows.
why: Weak rows are refreshed by the workload itself, so the global interval can stretch 2-4x (fact 3) with no extra refresh traffic; OS and controller change on existing DRAM.

title: Dead body-bias trick revived via printed back-gate planes
idea: Dynamic body biasing (DTMOS) died in bulk CMOS because the body-effect coefficient shrank and wells are huge capacitors. In a printed double-gate oxide TFT array, a printed global back-gate plane couples strongly to the thin channel. Hold the plane at -3 V during retention (high Vt, ultralow leakage) and swing it to 0 V only on the tile being accessed (low Vt, fast).
why: Decouples speed from leakage, so access devices can be fast and still retain for seconds. Cuts refresh ~100x on foil memory.

title: 22FDX eDRAM with back-gate retention bias on a U.S. line
idea: Fully depleted SOI gives every transistor an independent back gate with a ~80 mV/V body factor. Tape out a 1T1C (MIM-capacitor) eDRAM macro on GlobalFoundries 22FDX in Malta, NY via MPW. The array's back-gate well swings to -2 V during retention, raising access Vt ~160 mV, and returns to 0 V during access. MPW, design and test fit ~$700k over 20 months.
why: +160 mV of Vt at ~70 mV/dec cuts hold-state subthreshold leakage ~200x while keeping access current. It demonstrates refresh-light, DRAM-class embedded memory on a U.S. fab (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Locksmith's deadbolt: separate per-row hold gate on vertical channels
idea: A locksmith throws the deadbolt only when the house is empty. Each vertical access pillar gets a second gate on its back face, tied per row: idle rows hold it at -1.5 V for a very high threshold, and it is released to 0 V ~2 ns before that row activates, so the front wordline needs no negative off level and its GIDL disappears.
why: Separates 'hold' from 'switch': ~0.3 V higher idle threshold (about 5 decades less subthreshold leakage) without the GIDL penalty, cutting refresh ~5-10x and permitting a lower wordline high level.

title: Coulomb-blockade silicon dot holds bit behind charging energy
idea: Box: few-electron Si quantum dot (<3 nm) storage x wordline-gated tunnel barrier access x single-electron-transistor electrometer sensing x in-array x SOI x oxidation-thinned nanowire. The dot's charging energy (>10 kT at room temperature for sub-3 nm dots) blocks electron escape until the wordline lowers the barrier.
why: Charge per bit drops from ~30,000 e- to ~10 e-, slashing CV2 (fact 10) and sidestepping the capacitor wall (fact 1). Room-temperature variability is speculative.

title: Invert strain engineering: heavy-valley transport suppresses source-drain tunneling
idea: Substitute mobility-boosting strain with the opposite: uniaxial compressive stress along a <100> channel fills the Si valleys whose heavy longitudinal mass (0.92 m0) points along transport. Direct source-to-drain tunneling at 6-8 nm gate length then falls exponentially, while on-current drops only ~2x.
why: Lets the access transistor shrink below ~10 nm gate length without a tunneling-leakage floor: ~10-100x lower direct-tunneling leakage, which helps both density and refresh.

title: Maxwell-Wagner bilayer capacitor back-fills leaked charge from interface reservoir
idea: Effect: interfacial (Maxwell-Wagner-Sillars) polarization, i.e., dielectric absorption. The cell capacitor is a high-k/low-conductivity bilayer engineered so interface charge accumulates over ms after a write and re-emerges as the node droops, like a capacitor's recovery voltage; a reset pulse on writes clears ghost charge from the previous value.
why: Retention x2-5 without a better transistor (fact 3). Risk: data-history ghosting and slow charging.

title: Ephemeral-memory cloud instances priced below standard RAM
idea: Reverse the memory guarantee into a product: cloud providers sell VM memory under a published 'touch-within-N-ms' contract (data preserved only if accessed or rewritten within, say, 32 ms) at a discount. These instances run on refresh-relaxed or refresh-off DRAM, including short-retention bins, and suit streaming inference, ETL and video pipelines that rewrite buffers continuously.
why: Monetizes refresh-free operation (fact 3) and lets lower-grade existing DRAM count as sellable capacity; a pricing and scheduler change, no fab.

title: Reduced-field storage levels when hot: low '1', raised plate
idea: Worse at 125 C: store '1' at full array voltage so field-enhanced generation and GIDL explode with heat. Flip: in hot mode store '1' at ~0.7 V and raise the cell plate to cut junction field, then recover signal with an offset-cancelled sense amp; leakage falls exponentially while charge falls only linearly.
why: Hot leakage (fact 3) down 5-10x and CV2 energy (fact 10) down ~40% in the hot regime.

title: Eliminate heat-driven leakage: thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier cooler under array
idea: Sputter or co-evaporate thin-film Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 thermoelectric couples into the substrate or interposer beneath the memory array, pumping the cell region 15-25 C below the surrounding logic. Since leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C, cooling only the array extends retention 3-6x.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall 3-6x in hot HBM stacks beside GPUs; thin-film thermoelectrics are university processes; costs some Peltier power.

title: Countercurrent charge recycling between consecutively refreshed wordlines
idea: Fish gills and bird legs recover heat by countercurrent exchange; during refresh bursts a local switch links the falling wordline of row n to the rising wordline of row n+k so about half of the ~3 V VPP charge transfers before the pump tops up, and bitline restore charge is shared between subarrays refreshed in antiphase.
why: Wordline and bitline energy per refresh falls ~35-50% (~46 to ~25-30 fJ/bit), and the inefficient VPP pump load roughly halves, shrinking pump area in the periphery.

title: Wire-drawn superconducting persistent-current loops for cryogenic working memory
idea: Use superconducting wire-drawing know-how (NbTi/Nb3Sn) as thin-film Nb micro-loops where the bit is a circulating persistent current. Josephson-junction access switches write and read it at 4 K, next to quantum computers and cryo-CMOS.
why: Zero refresh: persistent currents never decay and junction-based access has no leakage, so refresh and hold power are both zero. This serves cryogenic compute without a warm-DRAM round trip.

title: Redox molecules as both selector and storage in crossbars
idea: IFR: the bit's own chemistry is the switch. Self-assemble a monolayer of multi-state redox molecules (ferrocene/porphyrin triads with ~0.5 V spaced oxidation potentials) between crossbar electrodes; oxidation stores charge, the discrete redox potentials give built-in threshold selectivity, and an insulating alkyl tether sets retention.
why: Constraint: each layer is a sub-5 nm monolayer between two lines, so 2 bits per site across several stacked crossbar layers targets ~10x density with only deposition and DUV lines.

title: Plated-wire revival: coated bitline wires with strap-defined junctionless access
idea: Revive Univac's plated-wire memory, in which crossing word straps addressed a continuous film on a wire: coat vertical bitline wires conformally (ALD) with a thin junctionless semiconductor shell. Each horizontal wordline strap wraps the wire and gates, all around, a shell segment linking the wire to an adjacent ring capacitor, so transistors are defined by strap crossings rather than per-cell lithography or doping.
why: No implanted junctions means no junction leakage and no GIDL hot spots (fact 3); strap-defined devices suit multi-tier 3D (fact 2) and need fewer EUV layers (fact 4).

title: Microsecond laser seeded recrystallization makes single-grain stacked access transistors
idea: Time shift in thermal processing: deposit amorphous Si for each 3D-DRAM tier, then sweep a microsecond-pulse laser so melt fronts grow laterally from a seed opening, giving one grain per access transistor while the short melt keeps lower tiers below 450 C.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): grain-boundary-free silicon gives bulk-like low leakage for lateral access transistors across 26+ tiers using only Si, with no IGZO In/Ga.

title: Epitaxial CaF2 gate insulator: a crystal, not a glass
idea: Scale shift from amorphous oxide to an atom-by-atom lattice: grow single-crystal CaF2 (lattice-matched to Si within ~0.6%) as the access-transistor gate dielectric so the interface is nearly trap-free and gate tunnelling at ~1 nm EOT is lower than SiO2; fewer interface traps means fewer trap-assisted GIDL and VRT sites.
why: Leakage tail/VRT (fact 3) and voltage floor (fact 10, thinner EOT allows lower wordline voltage); Ca and F are abundant; risk is CaF2 epitaxy on 3D pillar sidewalls.

title: Swap 3D NAND roles: depreciated NAND lines build 3D DRAM
idea: Reverse 3D NAND's roles in a depreciated 64-96-layer NAND line: deposit alternating thin poly-Si and oxide planes as usual, but fill the vertical hole with metal as a wordline gate wrapping each plane, so each plane segment becomes a lateral access transistor whose far end is recessed and filled with a lateral MIM capacitor. The <=5 nm poly planes are fully depleted, and laser anneal enlarges grains to cut leakage.
why: Attacks 'no manufacturable 3D DRAM' (fact 2) and capital intensity (fact 4) on depreciated NAND tools with no EUV; poly-channel leakage limits retention, so it suits a dense short-refresh tier.

title: Memory that rots on purpose: nanoimprinted foil for short-lived data
idea: Inverts 'memory must keep data until overwritten': roll-to-roll nanoimprint (~100 nm) 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on metal foil with small leaky cells (1-10 ms retention, no refresh circuitry), laminate ~50 foils into a block, and let accelerators store only activations, gradients and KV pages consumed within the retention window, recomputing on rare loss.
why: Roll-to-roll layers cost ~$1-5/m2 versus ~$10,000/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so even at ~30x lower density it is ~100x cheaper per GB for transient data; trade-off: no long-term storage, ~100 ns-1 us access.

title: Idle power budget of 1 mW per GB: in-DRAM compaction before self-refresh
idea: Limit: in self-refresh the die may refresh only the rows it truly needs. On self-refresh entry, an on-die engine applies zero, pattern and base-delta compression to each subarray, packs the data into fewer subarrays with in-DRAM row copy, and stops refreshing the vacated subarrays. It decompresses on exit.
why: Fact 3: AI and server data compress ~2-3x, so self-refresh energy falls ~50-65% for idle devices.

title: Global pulse self-restore: whole-die refresh in one nanosecond broadcast
idea: Time shift from serial row-by-row refresh (8k REF commands per 64 ms) to one die-wide pulse: each cell adds a tiny gain transistor gated by its own storage node, with its drain on a shared 'restore' mesh; pulsing the mesh to VARY for ~2 ns tops up every node still reading '1' (gain device on) and leaves '0' nodes untouched, with no wordline, bitline or sense-amp activity.
why: Refresh bandwidth loss (10-20%, fact 3) goes to ~0 and refresh energy falls ~20-50x because only cell charge moves, not bitlines; the 2T cell costs ~40% area, offset if it relaxes capacitor targets (fact 1).

title: Eliminate the 3 V wordline: negative-capacitance HZO access gate
idea: Insert an ALD Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 ferroelectric layer, capacitance-matched to an HfO2/SiO2 underlayer, into the access gate so it acts as an internal voltage amplifier with sub-60 mV/dec slope. The same off current is reached with a 1-1.5 V wordline swing, or the same swing gives ~100x lower leakage.
why: Wordline CV^2 energy cut 4-9x (fact 10) and charge-pump area removed (fact 7); hysteresis-free matching is the risk.

title: Negative-capacitance gate stack: beat 60 mV/decade to close the leak
idea: Inverts 'the Boltzmann 60 mV/dec limit fixes off-leakage for a given wordline swing': add a thin doped-HfO2 negative-capacitance layer to the access gate (as a voltage amplifier only, not storage) to reach ~40 mV/dec, so the same swing yields 10-100x lower Ioff or the same Ioff at ~2 V wordline.
why: Attacks both the leakage tail (fact 3) and the 3 V wordline floor (fact 10): ~10-30x longer retention or ~45% lower wordline CV2.

title: Electrician's circuit breaker: NbO2 threshold film in the access source
idea: A breaker stays open until demand trips it. A thin NbO2 insulator-metal-transition film sits in series with each access transistor's source contact: it stays insulating, blocking subthreshold leakage, until the low-Vt transistor is driven, then snaps metallic, giving an effectively steep slope so the wordline can swing ~1 V.
why: Hyper-FET action drops the wordline from a pumped 3 V to ~1 V (~9x on CV^2, more with no pump) while the insulating film doubles as a leakage blocker; risks are NbO2 off-resistance and threshold drift.

title: Hearing-aid tunnel-FET access device with sub-60 mV/dec switching
idea: Zinc-air hearing aids run near 1.2 V, which pushes designers toward band-to-band tunneling switches. Use a vertical heterojunction TFET (Ge source, Si channel in the pillar) as the access device: its modest on-current still charges 5 fF in ~10 ns, and its steep slope lets the wordline swing shrink while off-current falls to sub-fA.
why: Facts 3 and 10: wordline swing ~3 V to ~1.5 V (~4x less wordline CV^2) and ~10x smaller leakage tail; drain-side ambipolar leakage must be suppressed with asymmetric doping.

title: Detector-grade float-zone silicon cuts generation leakage and quartz dependence
idea: Build DRAM on crucible-free float-zone wafers of the kind used for radiation detectors, with ms-scale minority lifetime and very low metal content, nitrogen-doped for strength. FZ tops out at 200 mm, which suits 1990s tool sets.
why: SRH generation current scales with ni/tau, so junction leakage falls 3-10x. It also bypasses the Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucible chokepoint (>80%).

title: GaP epitaxy in existing storage contacts puts field in wide-gap material
idea: Box: standard cap x access with a Si/GaP heterojunction storage drain x standard SA x in-array x Si x selective GaP MOCVD inside the already-opened storage-node contact holes (zero added masks). GaP is lattice-matched to Si (0.4%) with a 2.26 eV gap, so the gate-edge high-field region sits where band-to-band tunneling is negligible.
why: GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling dominate the tail (fact 3); a wide-gap drain could cut them >10x with no new mask. Antiphase defects and thermal budget are the risk.

title: Sell the leaky dies: short-retention DRAM SKU for rewrite-heavy buffers
idea: Reverse the binning logic: dies that fail the 64 ms retention spec but pass at 8-16 ms, today scrapped or downgraded, become a 'fast-turnover' SKU for buffers that rewrite every row within milliseconds (AI activation and KV staging, video frames, packet buffers). The controller enforces a per-row touch deadline instead of refresh.
why: Raises usable supply from existing fabs by recovering retention-fallout yield (a few % of output) with no new tools, and drops refresh where it is wasted (fact 3).

title: Regenerative braking for bitlines: recycle refresh charge into the next subarray
idea: Electric vehicles recover braking energy instead of burning it in friction brakes. After a subarray's refresh, before equalization, connect its high-side bitlines through a charge-sharing switch matrix to the next subarray's bitlines so the next refresh starts part-charged, recovering a further ~25-40% of bitline CV^2 beyond normal equalization.
why: Bitline swing dominates the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy (fact 3); recycling could cut refresh energy 25-40% with no cell change.

title: BTI-recovery pulses scheduled into refresh slots
idea: Worse at 125 C: let bias-temperature instability creep the access-transistor Vt for 10 years until leakage or write speed fails. Flip: use each refresh slot for rows not being restored to apply a short reverse-polarity gate pulse that de-traps the BTI charge, holding Vt drift below ~10 mV over life.
why: Keeps the leakage tail (fact 3) and write margin stable over 10 years hot, avoiding guard-band overdesign.

title: Cell-membrane-mimetic molecular seal on oxide-FET back channels
idea: Lipid bilayers are only 5 nm thick yet nearly impermeable to ions; seal the exposed back channel of BEOL oxide access FETs with a densely packed fluoroalkyl phosphonic-acid monolayer (vapor-deposited at 120 C) capped by ALD Al2O3, blocking the O2/H2O adsorption that creates surface donor states and random-telegraph Vt jumps.
why: Targets variable retention time in oxide devices, cutting tail leakage and drift ~3-10x with no anneal.

title: Sacrificial canary rows give closed-loop refresh margin
idea: Profile each channel's 64 weakest rows at boot, fill them with known patterns, and refresh them 1.5x less often than data rows. Poll them every interval, so the first canary flip (from a temperature spike or VRT jump) immediately tightens the refresh rate for data rows. Controller firmware and validation cost under $300k.
why: Worst-case guardbanding becomes feedback, so data runs near its measured retention (2-4x the spec interval) on commodity parts (fact 3), at a cost of a few rows per channel.

title: Air-spacer drain overlap defuses the GIDL hot spot
idea: GIDL is set by the peak field where the wordline overlaps the storage-node junction, and it scales as exp(-B/F). Replace the gate dielectric in only the last ~5 nm of overlap with a sealed air spacer (k=1). This lowers the overlap field ~3-4x and leaves channel control untouched.
why: A 3x field cut lowers BTBT GIDL by several decades. GIDL is what limits deeper negative wordline off-bias, so this allows deeper off-bias and ~3-10x longer tail retention (fact 3). It also reduces wordline-to-node coupling relevant to row hammer (fact 9).

title: One-mask selective reoxidation thickens storage-side gate edge
idea: Box: standard cap x recessed access with asymmetric gate dielectric x SA x in-array x Si x one mask exposing only storage-side recess tops to an extra radical oxidation. Thicker dielectric only where the gate overlaps the storage junction lowers the field driving GIDL while channel oxide stays thin for drive.
why: GIDL is exponential in field; ~30% thicker edge oxide can cut it ~10x, extending refresh (fact 3) for one mask.

title: Hibernating banks with on-die thermoelectric torpor cooling
idea: Like hibernators that drop body temperature to slash metabolism, place thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier elements under each bank/HBM die region, pump heat from idle banks into active ones' sinks to hold idle banks 15-25 C cooler, and let the refresh controller stretch tREFI per bank from its temperature sensor.
why: Leakage roughly halves every 8-10 C, so idle banks get 2-4x longer refresh intervals, cutting refresh power (16-33% of idle) by ~50-75%.

title: Chill the memory, not the room: Peltier-pumped DRAM tier
idea: Inverts 'DRAM runs at whatever temperature the package gives it': a thin-film Bi2Te3 thermoelectric layer between the DRAM stack and the logic die pumps heat out of the DRAM dies to hold them ~25 C below the logic; retention roughly doubles per 10 C, so refresh rate drops ~5x.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth tax (fact 3) fall ~80% and row-hammer thresholds improve (fact 9); makes HBM-on-logic thermally cheaper. Cost is TEC power, partly offset by refresh savings.

title: RFID-cheap transistorless crosspoint capacitors with MIIM tunnel selectors
idea: Penny RFID tags use two-terminal tunnel structures. Replace the access transistor with a back-to-back metal-insulator-insulator-metal tunnel selector (~1e6-1e8 I-V nonlinearity) in a 4F^2 crosspoint of stacked capacitors; half-selected cells leak and disturb, giving ~1% raw BER that page coding absorbs.
why: Facts 2 and 4: no transistor means no lateral-transistor blocker for 3D and no EUV access layer, with 4F^2 stacked tiers for 2-4x density per mask; refresh is frequent, so it fits streaming and ephemeral data.

title: Self-assembled diode dots: block copolymers replace EUV for every cell
idea: Inverts 'lithography must define each access device': coat a PS-b-PDMS block copolymer guided by coarse 193 nm trenches into 10 nm-pitch dot arrays, then convert each dot by sequential infiltration synthesis into a vertical oxide Schottky diode atop a MIM nanocapacitor, mapping out defective dots at test.
why: Zero EUV layers (fact 4) and ~1 mask per tier at 10 nm pitch; with 8 tiers, ~100x lower cost per GB; trade-off is diode leakage forcing ms refresh and DSA defect remapping.

title: Contactless NEMS relay: tunneling-gap mechanical access switch
idea: Nanomechanical relays died from contact wear and stiction after 1e9-1e12 cycles. Never let the beam touch: an electrostatically pulled beam moves its tip from a 4 nm gap to a 1 nm gap against the storage-node pad, which switches electron tunneling current by ~1e9 without contact. A self-assembled-monolayer stopper serves only as a fail-safe.
why: No semiconductor in the off path, so retention is limited only by the capacitor dielectric and refresh is effectively eliminated. Because the switch never makes contact, the wear that killed relays never occurs.

title: Minify displacement to sub-angstrom: sliding-ferroelectric bilayer access gate
idea: Use bilayer hBN or 3R-MoS2 whose ~0.1 nm interlayer stacking slide flips out-of-plane polarization as the gate stack of a 2D-channel transistor, setting Vt non-volatilely. Switching is interlayer sliding with no ion motion or bond breaking, so there is no wake-up, fatigue or imprint mechanism.
why: Non-volatile 1T cell with potentially unlimited endurance, sub-1 V write, no capacitor and no refresh.

title: Storage node may touch no pn junction: MIS tunnel contact
idea: Limit: the storage node may not have a depletion junction to the substrate. Contact the capacitor through a ~1 nm Al2O3/SiO2 interlayer onto a fully depleted ultrathin-body channel. This metal-insulator-semiconductor contact passes write current by direct tunneling and eliminates the junction depletion volume, where SRH thermal generation and trap-assisted tunneling create the tail.
why: Fact 3: junction leakage is a dominant tail component. With no junction volume, worst-cell generation falls ~10-100x and refresh could stretch toward ~1 s.

title: Store the majority in the leak-sink state with row inversion flags
idea: Flip data polarity per row: at each write, on-die logic counts the bits and stores the row inverted whenever that places more bits in the discharged state the cells leak toward, recording one flag bit per 1 KB row. Zero-heavy real data then keeps 80-90% of bits in a state that cannot decay.
why: Refresh (fact 3): only charged cells can fail, so per-row failure probability drops 5-10x and the refresh interval stretches ~2-4x at the same ECC strength; <0.1% bit overhead.

title: Steer data into the discharged state on unmodified DRAM
idea: Flip data polarity from outside the chip: commodity DRAM mixes true-cell and anti-cell subarrays. Map them once per part number with retention tests, then have the controller XOR-invert data per address so zeros, the most common value, land as discharged charge in both cell types, replacing today's random scrambling with a polarity-aware mask.
why: Fewer charged cells means fewer cells that can fail, so ECC-protected refresh relaxes ~2x (fact 3); controller logic only, on existing chips.

title: Eliminate bulk thickness: 2 nm quantum-confined silicon body widens bandgap
idea: Thin SOI by repeated thermal oxidation and HF strip to a 2-3 nm body, where quantum confinement widens silicon's effective gap by ~0.3-0.5 eV and suppresses intrinsic carrier density 1e3-1e4x; build the access device in this film over a thick buried oxide. Only furnace oxidation and wet etch are needed.
why: Leakage drops ~1000x from bandgap widening while staying all-silicon and U.S.-manufacturable; mobility loss is tolerable because a cell needs only microamps.

title: Two-nanometre quantum-confined silicon body widens the access bandgap
idea: Box: cap x <=2.5 nm Si nanosheet access channel x SA x lateral 3D-stackable cell x epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattice x selective SiGe etch. Confinement raises the effective gap ~0.3-0.4 eV, dropping intrinsic carrier density ~100x and band-to-band tunneling sharply, while staying in silicon.
why: Order-of-magnitude cut in generation and GIDL leakage (fact 3) without new channel materials, compatible with Si/SiGe-stack 3D DRAM (fact 2).

title: Liquid-nitrogen CXL memory sleds with refresh switched off
idea: Box: unmodified 1T1C dies x standard access at 77 K x standard SA x CXL memory sled immersed in LN2 x Si x no fab change, LN2 piped from on-site air separation. At 77 K junction and subthreshold leakage drop >1e6x so refresh is disabled, and lower wire resistance trims I/O energy.
why: Removes refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3) and permits lower Vt/VPP (fact 10) for pooled capacity; helium-free cryogen. Cryocooling overhead limits it to dense pooled tiers.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory sleds where refresh switches off
idea: IFR: leakage frozen out. Put DRAM sleds in sealed 77 K LN2 baths fed by a shared data-center cryo plant, where junction and subthreshold leakage fall by many orders of magnitude so refresh is disabled and wire resistance drops ~5x.
why: Fact 3 and 5: removes refresh energy and bandwidth and lowers I/O energy; cryo overhead (~10 W per W removed) must be beaten by the lower heat produced, best for dense cold-data tiers.

title: Sous-vide sealing: channel epi and gate oxide grown without air break
idea: Sous-vide food is sealed before cooking so nothing can contaminate it. Replace the HF-last pre-gate clean with a cluster tool that grows a fresh selective epitaxial silicon skin on the access-channel surface (SiH4/HCl/H2) and oxidizes it in situ by radical oxidation without breaking vacuum, so the gate interface is born clean and never touches hydrofluoric acid.
why: Pristine interfaces cut trap-assisted leakage and Vt variation (fact 3) and remove HF baths and their waste stream, easing U.S. fab permitting (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Thin to widen: quantum-confined 2 nm channel raises effective bandgap
idea: Reverse the scaling instinct of keeping a thick body for less variability: thin the access-transistor body to ~2 nm Si (vertical fin or nanosheet), which raises the effective bandgap ~0.2-0.3 eV by quantum confinement. Band-to-band tunneling and thermal generation currents fall exponentially with the gap, and DRAM's modest on-current need absorbs the mobility loss.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10-100x lower GIDL/generation current stretches retention several-fold at the same Cs.

title: Schwann-cell spiral roll-up wraps gate-all-around around BEOL channels
idea: Schwann cells wrap axons in a compact spiral of membrane; deposit a strained bilayer (graded SiNx plus metal gate plus ALD dielectric) on a sacrificial layer beside each vertical oxide channel, then release it at room temperature so it rolls itself into a multi-turn gate-all-around shell.
why: Gives ideal GAA control (~62 mV/dec, low DIBL) on low-temperature channels without high-temperature conformal fills in narrow gaps, cutting off-current 10-100x at the same on-current.

title: Data that dies young gets no refresh: lifetime-tagged no-refresh banks
idea: Limit: refresh only bits that will outlive the retention window. The runtime tags allocations with a time-to-live and places short-lived ones (activations, attention scratch, gradient buffers overwritten every few ms) in banks with refresh disabled. A hardware lease timer raises an error if any data is read after its window.
why: Fact 3: a large share of AI training and inference DRAM traffic is short-lived. Taking those banks out of refresh recovers their share of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and of idle power.
